sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Subsistence Farming**: Practiced to meet family consumption needs with little or no surplus for market sale, characterized by low capital investment and primitive tools.
• **Commercial Farming**: Market-oriented farming utilizing high doses of modern inputs like HYV seeds, chemical fertilizers, insecticides, and machinery to achieve higher productivity.
• **Intensive Farming**: Characterized by high labor and capital input per unit of land, high dose of biochemical inputs, and irrigation to maximize yield in densely populated regions.
• **Extensive Farming**: Practiced on large tracts of land with low labor and capital input per unit area, resulting in lower per-hectare yield but high total output.

items.definition: A form of shifting cultivation practiced in North-East India where forests are cleared and burnt to enrich soil nutrients temporarily before moving to a new plot.
The agricultural practice of growing a single crop year after year on the same land, heavily prominent in plantation economies like tea, coffee, and rubber.
System of farming that relies on green manure, compost, biological pest control, and crop rotation, avoiding synthetic fertilizers and GMOs (e.g., Sikkim as 100% organic state).
A flagship scheme promoting organic farming through cluster approach and Participatory Guarantee System (PGS) certification to reduce input costs and ensure chemical-free food.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **North-Eastern India**: Dominance of Jhum (shifting) cultivation; transitioning to terrace cultivation due to soil degradation and government interventions.
• **North-West India (Punjab, Haryana, Western UP)**: Highly intensive commercial and mechanized farming driven by the Green Revolution, heavy tubewell irrigation, and MSP-backed wheat-paddy cycle.
• **Peninsular and Southern India**: Plantation farming hubs (tea in Assam/Nilgiris, coffee in Karnataka/Wayanad, rubber in Kerala) and dryland farming in interior Deccan plateau.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Extreme land fragmentation, heavy dependence on erratic monsoons, depletion of groundwater tables in intensive zones, and low capital formation in subsistence sectors.
• **Policy Interventions**: National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA), Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY), digital agriculture initiatives, and promotion of Natural Farming (Bharatiya Prakritik Krishi Paddhati).

items.title: Mnemonic for Shifting Cultivation Names Across India
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "JD-BP-VK" -> Jhum (North-East), Dahiya/Bewar (Madhya Pradesh), Podu (Andhra Pradesh/Odisha), Kumari (Western Ghats), Valre/Waltre (Rajasthan).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Regional vernacular names of slash-and-burn agriculture.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Direct matching questions in UPSC Prelims regarding indigenous farming terms.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Intensity of farming is inversely proportional to landholding size and directly proportional to population density and irrigation availability.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often conflates 'Intensive Subsistence Farming' with 'Commercial Farming' in the Indo-Gangetic plains. Remember that despite high chemical input use in Punjab/Haryana, the underlying structural driver in most of India remains smallholding subsistence, except in specific commercial/plantation enclaves.

Mains Value Addition: Quote Economic Survey data regarding the average operational landholding size dropping below 1.08 hectares and link it directly to the viability of subsistence versus cooperative/contract farming.

keyTakeaways: Farming types in India range from primitive subsistence and shifting cultivation to capital-intensive commercial plantations and mixed farming systems.
Geographical distribution is heavily dictated by topography, rainfall, colonial legacies, and the regional adoption of Green Revolution technologies.
Contemporary policy focus is shifting towards sustainable, organic, and natural farming models to counter ecological degradation in intensive farming zones.
